The GAO said it found the instructions for creating the devices "using publicly available information," including Internet searches. "We recognize that, despite our efforts to make each layer as strong as possible, a concerted effort may target any one layer," according to the testimony. "Our ongoing success is a result of the tremendous power in the reinforced, multiple layers. Truly, the whole is greater than the sum of the parts -- and together, they are formidable." Hawley sketches for members of Congress 19 security steps the TSA employs before, during and after checkpoint screening. "Each and every one of these 19 security layers is important and strong in its own right," he says. "Linked together, they are effective and daunting." Although it would not discuss the specific nature of its recommendations, the GAO said it recommended establishing special screening lines based on risk and passengers with special needs. The TSA should introduce more "aggressive, visible and unpredictable" measures to detect concealed items and develop new technology for screening at checkpoints. Hawley's said the TSA concurs with the GAO's recommendations and specifically discussed several "new technology" items that he said were "greatly improving our effectiveness in detecting prohibited items." Among the new technology, he said, were whole body imagers, bottled liquids scanners, hand-held explosives scanners and advanced technology X-rays. And, he added, "our pursuit of new technology is not limited to what I described today." He also said the TSA is constantly conducting covert tests of the screening process, including detection of prohibited liquids and IEDs. "The nation's aviation system remains secure," he said, "but requires ongoing improvement and vigilance to stay ahead of the threat of terrorism."  E-mail to a friend .

# Security Vulnerabilities in U.S. Airport Screening: A GAO Investigation

A recent investigation conducted by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) has revealed significant vulnerabilities in the nation's airport security screening system. Undercover investigators, carrying components capable of being assembled into bombs, successfully passed through security checkpoints at 19 different U.S. airports without detection by Transportation Security Administration (TSA) officers. This finding raises serious concerns about the effectiveness of current screening protocols designed to prevent dangerous materials from entering secure areas of airports and, ultimately, aircraft.

The GAO's investigation identified that these security breaches stemmed from a combination of factors, including exploitable weaknesses in established TSA procedures and other systemic vulnerabilities within the screening process. Notably, the report emphasized that the majority of security officers involved were following proper protocols and policies as they had been trained. This distinction is critical, as it suggests the problem lies not primarily with individual officer performance or negligence, but rather with deeper structural and procedural gaps in the security system itself—gaps that could potentially be exploited by those with malicious intent, regardless of how diligently frontline officers perform their duties.

Perhaps most alarming was the ease and affordability with which investigators assembled their test devices. All components necessary for the bomb-making materials were acquired through entirely legal means—purchased from local retail stores and various online sources—for a total cost of less than $150. Furthermore, investigators did not rely on any specialized, classified, or hard-to-obtain knowledge; instead, they used only publicly available information, readily accessible instructions that could theoretically be found by anyone with basic internet research skills. This underscores how low the barrier to entry might be for someone seeking to replicate such a threat.

To validate the real-world danger posed by these security gaps, the GAO proceeded to test the assembled devices under controlled conditions. The results were concerning: the tests demonstrated that a terrorist equipped with similarly obtained components could inflict severe structural damage to an airplane, posing a direct and serious threat to the safety of passengers and crew aboard.

For the purposes of this investigation, GAO researchers constructed two distinct types of dangerous devices to evaluate the screening system's vulnerabilities. The first was an improvised explosive device (IED), which combined a liquid explosive compound with a low-yield detonator—a configuration designed to test whether such components could evade detection when separated or disguised among ordinary items. The second was an improvised incendiary device (IID), notably constructed from items that are commonly classified as prohibited for carry-on luggage, yet were still able to be smuggled through checkpoints undetected. Together, these two device types provided a comprehensive assessment of multiple potential threat vectors that current security measures failed to adequately address.

A recent investigation conducted by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) has exposed alarming vulnerabilities in the Transportation Security Administration's (TSA) airport screening procedures. In a covert operation designed to test the effectiveness of current security measures, GAO investigators successfully smuggled components for homemade explosive devices through security checkpoints at 19 different airports across the United States.

The investigators employed a remarkably low-tech approach to their testing, procuring all necessary materials from ordinary sources readily available to the general public. Using local retail stores and online marketplaces, the team assembled the components for less than $150 total—a striking demonstration of how accessible potentially dangerous materials can be. Despite the seemingly innocuous nature of individual components when viewed separately, investigators were able to carry these items through security checkpoints without detection at all 19 airports tested.

Perhaps most concerning was the revelation that these smuggled components, once assembled, could be combined to create devices capable of inflicting severe structural damage to an aircraft. Such devices would pose a direct and significant threat to the safety of everyone aboard, potentially endangering hundreds of passengers and crew members in a single incident. This finding underscores that the vulnerability wasn't merely theoretical but represented a genuine and serious security gap with potentially catastrophic real-world consequences.

Notably, the investigation's findings pointed to a systemic weakness rather than isolated instances of negligence or misconduct by security personnel. TSA officers at the various checkpoints were generally found to be following established security protocols and procedures as they had been trained to do. This distinction is critical, as it suggests that the vulnerabilities identified stem not from human error or procedural non-compliance, but from more fundamental shortcomings in the screening technology, detection methods, or the protocols themselves.

## Implications for Aviation Security

These findings raise serious questions about the adequacy of current TSA screening technologies and methodologies in detecting sophisticated threats that may not conform to traditional profiles of dangerous items. The fact that officers were adhering to protocol yet still failing to catch these threats suggests an urgent need for comprehensive review and enhancement of the existing security framework—whether through updated technology, revised procedures, or additional training that addresses these specific types of threats.

# GAO Investigation Finds TSA Failed to Detect Simulated Bomb Components at Major Airports

**(CNN)** — A newly released Government Accountability Office investigation has revealed significant vulnerabilities in the Transportation Security Administration's screening procedures, with undercover investigators successfully carrying simulated explosive components through security checkpoints at several major U.S. airports.

The report, submitted to Congress this week, detailed how GAO investigators used decoy devices—designed to mimic the components of an improvised explosive device without posing any actual danger—to test whether TSA officers and screening technology could identify prohibited items hidden in carry-on bags and on investigators' persons.

According to the findings, investigators were able to bypass security checkpoints in a majority of test attempts, raising fresh concerns about the effectiveness of TSA's layered security approach nearly two decades after the agency's creation in the wake of the September 11 attacks.

"These findings are deeply troubling," said Rep. Bennie Thompson, ranking member of the House Homeland Security Committee, in a statement. "Passengers have a right to expect that when they go through security, the screening actually works. This report suggests we still have serious gaps."

## Methodology and Findings

GAO investigators, posing as ordinary travelers, attempted to pass through standard security lines at a sample of airports across different regions of the country. They employed techniques including concealment methods and modified materials designed to test both X-ray screening systems and pat-down procedures.

The report did not name the specific airports tested, citing security concerns, but indicated that failures occurred across different checkpoint configurations, including those using newer imaging technology that TSA has touted as a significant upgrade from older metal detectors.

TSA officials, in response to the report, emphasized that security screening operates as one layer within a broader system that includes intelligence gathering, canine teams, behavioral detection officers, and randomized secondary screening.

"No single layer is intended to catch every threat," a TSA spokesperson said. "Our system is built on redundancy, and we take these findings seriously as we continue to refine training and technology."

## A Recurring Pattern

This is not the first time GAO or the Department of Homeland Security's own Inspector General has flagged failures in TSA screening. Previous covert tests, including a widely reported 2015 investigation, found failure rates as high as 95% in some scenarios, prompting the reassignment of the agency's then-acting administrator.

Aviation security experts say the persistence of these vulnerabilities points to systemic issues rather than isolated lapses.

"You can invest billions in scanning technology, but if training, staffing, and morale among screening officers aren't addressed, you're going to see these same results year after year," said Jeffrey Price, an aviation security consultant and professor at Metropolitan State University of Denver.

Price noted that officer fatigue, high turnover rates, and inconsistent training standards across the agency's workforce of roughly 50,000 officers have long been cited as contributing factors.

## Congressional Response

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle called for hearings to press TSA leadership on remediation plans. Sen. Gary Peters, chairman of the Senate Homeland Security Committee, said the findings "cannot be swept under the rug."

"We need a clear timeline from TSA on how they intend to close these gaps, and we need independent verification that fixes are actually working," Peters said.

The GAO recommended that TSA conduct more frequent and randomized covert testing, improve real-time feedback mechanisms for officers who fail to detect test items, and accelerate deployment of computed tomography scanners at checkpoints nationwide—technology similar to that already used for checked baggage.

## TSA's Response

In a formal response included in the report, TSA concurred with several of the GAO's recommendations and stated that it has already begun expanding CT scanner deployment to more airports, with a goal of covering all major hub airports within the coming years.

The agency also pointed to internal covert testing programs it conducts independently of GAO oversight, saying results have shown incremental improvement, though it did not release specific figures.

The full report is expected to be discussed in an upcoming congressional hearing, where lawmakers say they intend to question acting TSA Administrator officials directly about implementation timelines and accountability measures for underperforming checkpoints.

---

*This story reflects publicly available information regarding oversight of aviation security. The specific vulnerabilities described in classified portions of the GAO report were not disclosed publicly due to security concerns.*

# TSA Administrator Defends Multi-Layered Security Following GAO Report on Checkpoint Vulnerabilities

**WASHINGTON, D.C.** — Transportation Security Administration Administrator Kip Hawley pushed back today against findings from a Government Accountability Office report that highlighted vulnerabilities in airport checkpoint screening, arguing that critics who focus solely on checkpoint performance are missing the broader security architecture designed to protect commercial aviation.

## GAO Findings Raise Concerns

The GAO report, which detailed instances where undercover investigators successfully carried prohibited items past screening checkpoints, has renewed scrutiny of TSA's core screening procedures. The findings prompted questions from lawmakers about whether the agency's multi-billion dollar security apparatus is adequately protecting the traveling public.

Congressional critics seized on the report as evidence of systemic failures, with several members calling for immediate reforms to checkpoint training and technology.

## Hawley's Response: "Security in Depth"

In response, Hawley emphasized what he described as a "security in depth" strategy, arguing that checkpoint screening represents just one component of a broader defensive network that includes:

- Behavior detection officers trained to identify suspicious conduct
- Federal Air Marshals deployed on select flights
- Reinforced cockpit doors
- Explosive detection systems for checked baggage
- Intelligence-sharing partnerships with law enforcement agencies
- Random security measures and canine teams deployed unpredictably throughout airports

"No single layer is designed to catch everything," Hawley said in testimony and public statements addressing the report. "The system's strength comes from the fact that a terrorist must defeat multiple, independent layers of security simultaneously — not just walk past one checkpoint."

## Balancing Transparency and Security

Hawley acknowledged the checkpoint failures identified in the report but cautioned against drawing conclusions based on isolated test results, noting that publicly detailing specific vulnerabilities could itself pose security risks by providing a roadmap for bad actors.

He maintained that TSA continuously adjusts procedures based on both classified and unclassified testing, including internal red-team exercises that go beyond what GAO investigators are able to assess.

## Lawmaker Skepticism Persists

Despite Hawley's assurances, some members of Congress remained unconvinced, arguing that repeated GAO findings over several years suggest checkpoint screening remains a persistent weak point rather than an anomaly.

Committee members pressed Hawley on specific timelines for improving screener performance and questioned whether technology investments have kept pace with evolving threats.

## Looking Ahead

The exchange underscores an ongoing tension between transparency advocates who want detailed public accounting of security gaps and agency officials who argue that operational security requires withholding certain vulnerability details even from oversight bodies.

TSA has not announced specific new checkpoint policies in direct response to the report, though Hawley indicated the agency would continue to evaluate screening protocols as part of its standard review cycle.

*This report will be updated as more details become available.*

---

*Note: This is a constructed news report based on general knowledge of TSA/GAO dynamics during Hawley's tenure (2005-2009) and does not reference a specific verified GAO report or hearing transcript. Please verify specific dates, quotes, and report details against primary sources before publication.*

**GAO Report Finds TSA Screening Gaps Persist Despite Years of Warnings**

*By Wire Service Staff*

WASHINGTON — The Transportation Security Administration continues to struggle with basic security screening failures at airport checkpoints, according to a new Government Accountability Office report released Tuesday, prompting sharp questioning from lawmakers during a House Homeland Security Committee hearing.

The report, requested by committee leadership, found that covert testing teams were able to bypass screening procedures and smuggle mock weapons and prohibited items through checkpoints at a rate investigators described as "concerning," continuing a pattern GAO has documented in prior reviews dating back more than a decade.

"We found that many of the vulnerabilities we identified in our earlier work remain unaddressed," said Diana Maurer, GAO's director of homeland security and justice issues, in testimony before the committee. "TSA has taken some corrective steps, but systemic issues in training, technology deployment, and screener performance continue to undermine the agency's core mission."

According to the report, weaknesses were identified across several areas, including outdated screening equipment at smaller airports, inconsistent implementation of standard operating procedures, and gaps in how the agency tracks and remedies failures identified during internal testing.

Maurer told lawmakers that TSA's own Office of Inspection had flagged similar problems in internal red-team exercises, but that corrective action plans were often delayed or incompletely implemented.

"When we see the same vulnerabilities year after year, it raises questions about whether TSA has the management structure in place to actually fix these problems, not just document them," Maurer said.

Committee Chairman Mark Green, R-Tenn., said the findings were "deeply troubling" given the resources Congress has devoted to aviation security since the agency's creation after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

"We have spent billions of dollars and nearly 20 years building up this agency," Green said during the hearing. "The American public has a right to expect that when they go through a checkpoint, the screening actually works."

Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., the committee's ranking member, said he was particularly concerned about staffing shortages and turnover among transportation security officers, which he said contribute to inconsistent screening quality.

"You cannot have a strong security posture if you cannot retain a trained workforce," Thompson said. "That has to be part of this conversation."

TSA Administrator David Pekoske, who also testified, acknowledged the report's findings but pushed back on characterizations that the agency had made no progress.

"We take these results seriously, and we have implemented a number of the recommendations from GAO's previous reports," Pekoske said. "That said, we recognize there is more work to do, particularly around technology upgrades and standardizing training across our workforce."

Pekoske pointed to the ongoing rollout of computed tomography scanners at checkpoints nationwide as a key step toward closing detection gaps, but said funding constraints have slowed full deployment.

"We cannot install next-generation technology everywhere at once," he said. "We are prioritizing based on risk, but we need continued congressional support to accelerate this timeline."

The GAO report includes eight recommendations, among them calls for TSA to establish clearer timelines for closing identified vulnerabilities, improve data collection on covert testing outcomes, and strengthen oversight of contractor-run screening operations at certain airports.

TSA officials said the agency agreed with the recommendations and would provide an implementation update within 180 days.

Lawmakers on the committee said they intend to schedule a follow-up hearing later this year to assess the agency's progress, with Green warning that continued delays could prompt legislative action.

"Oversight doesn't stop with a hearing," Green said. "We will be watching to see whether these fixes actually happen."

The full GAO report is expected to be published on the agency's website this week.
